title: Spotigo : Spot it , report it , fix it!
pitch: Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.

 Spotigo — Project Story 

 A WebMCP-powered civic agent that turns human intent into safe, executable web actions. 

 
 Describe the problem. Let the agent handle the workflow. Keep the human in control of the part that matters. 
 

 Inspiration 

 The web already has the services people need. The friction is almost never "does this exist" — it's "can I get from what I want to say to the specific form this particular website expects." A citizen who sees a pothole thinks someone should report this , not let me figure out which municipal category this falls under, whether it's already been reported, and how to phrase it correctly. The problem exists. The digital service to fix it probably exists too. The gap is entirely in connecting human intent to that workflow — and that gap is exactly what WebMCP is positioned to close. 

 My first idea wasn't civic reporting at all — it was an accessible, voice-first grocery storefront. Before building much of it, I checked what was already in the WebMCP showcase and found Verdant Market already occupying that lane: "browse groceries and build a shared cart with an agent." Rather than build a variation on an existing reference app, I kept the one pattern worth keeping — the agent prepares, the human confirms — and moved it to a domain where getting that confirmation wrong actually matters: civic reporting, where the output is a public record, not a grocery order. 

 What it does 

 A citizen describes a civic issue by voice or text — "there's a huge pothole near my office" — and an agent turns that into a real, trackable report, gated by explicit human confirmation at the one step that counts. 

 Spotigo registers 10 WebMCP tools in the browser through document.modelContext , deliberately shaped as a workflow rather than a flat list: 

 
 
 Stage 
 Tools 
 
 
 
 Understand 
 describe_issue_accessibly , report_civic_issue 
 
 
 Validate 
 check_duplicate_reports , list_nearby_reports 
 
 
 Explain 
 read_report_summary 
 
 
 Authorize 
 confirm_submission , acknowledge_safety_guidance 
 
 
 Act 
 submit_report 
 
 
 Recover / Track 
 undo_last_action , get_report_status 
 
 

 A real pass through it: the agent structures "huge pothole near my office" into a draft — category pothole , description, resolved location — checks it against nearby reports and comes back with a graded confidence assessment (not a flat yes/no), then reads the draft back in plain language: "I'm about to report a large pothole at this location with this description. Submit it?" Only after an explicit confirm: true does submit_report become callable, returning a real tracking ID the citizen can check later with get_report_status . 

 How we built it 

 Zero build step, zero runtime dependencies, static files only — deliberate, so the WebMCP layer itself stays the thing under inspection, not something buried under framework abstraction. 

 One execution path, not two. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing WebMCP tools call the same tool.execute() closures — there's no separate "demo path" for the agent. If a judge opens the on-page Tool Tester and fires submit_report before confirming, they get the identical rejection an agent would get, because it's literally the same code running either way. 

 Ten tools, not one do_everything() . It would have been simpler to expose a single submit_report(details) function and let a system prompt handle the reasoning. That would hide exactly the part worth demonstrating — the validation, the safety boundaries, the point where understanding what someone wants stops being enough to act on it. Decomposing the workflow into explicit stages made the tool surface mirror the actual application logic instead of papering over it. 

 Intent is not authorization. The agent can understand the issue, check for duplicates, and explain what it's about to do — none of that authorizes submit_report . That gate is enforced in code: confirm: "yes" is truthy in JavaScript but explicitly rejected, because a loose check could let an ambiguous model output pass as authorization. Only strict confirm: true opens the gate. 

 The gate adapts to risk. Routine issues get one confirmation. Safety-critical ones — a downed power line, a suspected gas leak — route through a distinct acknowledge_safety_guidance step first, and lose the normal undo safety net once submitted. A pothole and a live wire aren't the same category of decision, and treating them identically would have been the easier, lazier design. 

 A second, separate experiment. server.js and server/ implement a persistent, authenticated MCP service for agents connecting outside the browser — real action storage, ownership isolation, rate limiting, a fail-closed authority resolver. It is explicitly not part of the deployed judged demo. I kept that line hard rather than implying a backend was live when it wasn't. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Choosing what not to build. The competitive check that killed the grocery idea happened before most of the code existed, which made it cheap. That ordering — research first, fall in love with the implementation second — was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. 

 Making confirmation a real boundary, not a suggestion. Getting the strict-boolean check right ( confirm: true vs. anything merely truthy) sounds trivial until you consider that an LLM producing "yes" or 1 instead of true is a completely plausible failure mode, and a loose check would have let it silently authorize a submission. 

 A Windows path bug invisible in my own dev loop. Automated smoke tests passed cleanly in my Linux sandbox and failed immediately on the actual Windows machine, with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME — Node's dynamic import() requires a proper file:// URL on Windows; a raw path like D:\...\app.js doesn't qualify, even though the POSIX equivalent works fine elsewhere.
